newsitem.title: INDIA: Relatives of Western hostages appeal to Kashmiris.
newsitem.headline: Relatives of Western hostages appeal to Kashmiris.

text.p: Relatives of three Western tourists taken hostage 15 months ago pleaded tearfully with Kashmiris on Monday to help trace the missing men in India's troubled Jammu and Kashmir state.

"We have come over to Kashmir to appeal to you, the people of Kashmir, for your help in tracing our sons and husbands," Bob Wells, father of British hostage Paul Wells, told a news conference in the state's summer capital, Srinagar.
Paul Wells, fellow-Briton Keith Mangan and Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs were captured on July 4, 1995 by the shadowy militant Al-Faran group while trekking in southern Kashmir.

Childs escaped on July 8 but Al-Faran the same day captured German Dirk Hasert and Norwegian Hans Ostroe. The latter's beheaded body was found in August 1995 while the other four -- Wells, Mangan, Hutchings and Hasert -- remained in Al-Faran hands.

Apart from the senior Wells, the news conference was attended by Paul Wells' girlfriend, Catherine Mosley, Hutchings' wife Jane Schelley and Mangan's wife Julie. Mangan's parents, Charles and Mavis Mangan, were also present.
All four women were dressed in local traditional "salwar kameez" (tunic and loose trousers).
"They (the hostages) came here to visit this beautiful country and to make friends... but instead they have been taken hostage, caught up in a political fight they were not part of," Wells said.
Kashmir has been the cause of two of the three wars India has fought with Pakistan since the nations gained independence from Britain in 1947.

Since 1990, dozens of separatist groups in Kashmir, the only Moslem majority state in predominantly Hindu India, have been fighting for complete independence or merger with Pakistan. The violence has killed at least 20,000 people.

"We will continue to call on the Pakistani government... Prime Minister (Benazir) Bhutto to remind her that she said that she was willing to help in every way possible," said Schelley, a schoolteacher.
"We hope the newly-elected government of Farooq Abdullah will make it a top priority to find out information based on rumours of sighting (of the hoistages)," she added.
Jammu and Kashmir state Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah said on Saturday he had reports the four tourists were still alive.
Authorities have had no contact with Al-Faran since last November, and diplomats said they have no firm indication whether the hostages are dead or alive.
In June, authorities used sniffer dogs to scour a forest where a captured militant said he believed the hostages had been buried after being killed last year. The search turned up no clues.
Mangan's father, tearful and looking tired, held up a photograph released by Al-Faran last year showing his son, injured, in captivity.
"We found this photo was a cruel hoax. Please, please don't let it happen for real," he said.
The relatives have been brought to Kashmir by a British television company which is making a documentary film depicting the hostage saga.
"We won't go away until we have answers about the case," Schelley said.
"It is a real nightmare living without Keith, I will still wait for him," Mangan's wife Julie said.
